items.title: Augustus claimed to have 'restored the Republic' in 27 BCE
items.claim: How did Augustus describe his own constitutional position?

options.text: He claimed to have 'restored the Republic' in his Res Gestae (the inscription set up at his mausoleum) — taking the title 'princeps' (first citizen) and refusing the title rex; in reality he held most magisterial powers and military command

items.reveal:
Octavian (Caesar's adopted heir) defeated Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE he made a show of restoring power to the Senate and was given the name Augustus ('revered'). He held tribunician power, imperium (military command) over the key provinces, and the title princeps senatus.

The Res Gestae Divi Augusti — 'The Achievements of the Divine Augustus' — was a long inscription set up at his death (14 CE) listing his deeds. It claims constitutional propriety throughout.

The Republic was, in effect, over. The Principate (early empire) lasted until the crises of the third century. The pretence of republican forms outlasted Augustus by centuries.
items.why: Political systems can hollow out while keeping their old names. Augustus's 'restored Republic' was already an autocracy in everything but name — a useful case in how institutional language can mask transformation.

items.title: The Korean War killed around 3 million people
items.claim: What was the death toll of the Korean War (June 1950-July 1953)?

options.text: Estimates centre around 3 million dead, mostly Korean civilians; nearly 37,000 US, around 1,000 British and Commonwealth, and over 400,000 Chinese troops killed
Comparable to WWI losses for the Allies

items.reveal:
North Korea invaded south of the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950. UN forces under General MacArthur landed at Inchon (September 1950) and pushed to the Yalu River; China entered in October-November.

The armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953. There has never been a peace treaty — the two Koreas are still technically at war. Pyongyang was reduced by US bombing to perhaps 25% of its buildings; an estimated 20% of North Korea's population died.

In the US, sandwiched between WWII and Vietnam, it became 'the forgotten war' despite high casualties.
items.why: Conflict casualties are not just about combatant deaths. Korea's civilian toll, the bombing intensity and the legacy of an unresolved war shape East Asia today — but rarely feature in Cold War textbooks.

items.title: Enclosure transferred millions of acres to private hands
items.claim: How much land was affected by Parliamentary enclosure (c. 1750-1850)?

options.text: Around 7 million acres — roughly a fifth of England — was enclosed by some 4,000 individual Acts of Parliament between 1750 and 1850
Enclosure was rare and ended in the 16th century

items.reveal:
Earlier enclosure (16th-17th centuries) had been informal and contested (Kett's Rebellion 1549). Parliamentary enclosure required individual Acts, with commissioners surveying and reallocating land in compact private holdings.

Common rights to graze, gather wood, glean and forage were extinguished. J. L. and Barbara Hammond's 'The Village Labourer' (1911) emphasised dispossession; later historians (J. M. Neeson, 'Commoners' 1993) revived the case for serious social impact.

The General Enclosure Acts of 1801 and 1845 streamlined the process. By 1900 the English commons were almost gone — though the Commons Preservation Society (1865) saved spaces like Hampstead Heath and Epping Forest.
items.why: The transition to industrial capitalism had a rural component. Enclosure freed up labour for cities and consolidated land for improved farming — at the cost of displacing a way of life that contemporaries actually missed.
